raw_case_text:
A 44-year-old Caucasian female with branchio-oto-renal (BOR) syndrome, who received a renal transplant from a deceased donor 20 years ago, came to the outpatient clinic complaining of bilateral progressive vision loss over the past 11 months (worse in her right eye, and at night), associated to central scotoma, without improvement when her lens prescription was updated. She did not report any other ocular symptoms such as pain or epiphora. Her visual acuity was 20/50 (right eye) and 20/80 (left eye). Slit lamp examination revealed corneal scars (sequelae from a refractive surgery) as well as diffuse and mild corneal opacities in both eyes. The fundoscopy showed a diffuse rarefaction of the retinal pigment epithelium, compatible with high myopia (Fig. 1). There were no signs of intraocular inflammation or infection on clinical examination. At this point, her visual acuity decreased to 20/400 (right eye) and 20/200 (left eye) without any clinically identifiable ocular disease. Electroretinography showed signs of ischemia, especially in the internal retina (Fig. 2A). Her current immunosuppressive treatment was tacrolimus, azathioprine and prednisone. In the individual patient history, she reported a refractive surgery to correct the high degree of myopia in both eyes 20 years ago, and also previous unprotected sex. 
A VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) test was ordered and the titer was 1: 2,048 and a positive treponemal test (fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption - FTA/ABS) was noted. The patient was admitted to the hospital for further tests and treatment. On the physical examination, she was in good health and had a discreet maculopapular erythematous rash on both palms, which spread to thoracic areas. She had no detected lesions in the genital region, abdominal masses, lymph node enlargements or branchial cleft cysts, neurologic deficits, or cardiovascular abnormalities. At admission, her blood creatinine was 1.5 g/dL. A confirmatory VDRL titer showed 1:512 and the FTA/ABS was positive. Others tests for HIV, hepatitis B and C were negative. Computed tomography of the brain was normal. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed a lymphocytic pleocytosis with the presence of 66.3 cells/ microL (100% lymphocytes), normal glucose and protein. VDRL was positive, but the titer decreased to 1/4 of the initial values and Cryptococcus antigens were negative. After the diagnosis of neuro-syphilis associated to retinopathy (bilateral vision loss associated to abnormalities seen at the electroretinography), the patient was treated with penicillin G (24 million IU/day) for 14 days. A few days after the penicillin was initiated, the patient reported a partial improvement of her visual acuity, although fundoscopy and electroretinography showed no differences in relation to the initial values. Four months after treatment, there was a partial improvement of the electroretinographic parameters (Fig. 2B), and in her last evaluation performed 6 months after treatment, she was asymptomatic, with a visual acuity of 20/40 in her right eye and 20/30 in her left eye. The VDRL titer was 1: 256.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old female renal transplant recipient with branchio-oto-renal syndrome presented with an 11-month history of progressive bilateral vision loss (worse in the right eye and at night) and central scotomas.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 11 months, the patient experienced painless progressive bilateral visual loss, nyctalopia, and central scotomas unimproved by refraction, with visual acuity declining from 20/50 OD and 20/80 OS to 20/400 OD and 20/200 OS.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of branchio-oto-renal (BOR) syndrome, deceased-donor kidney transplantation 20 years ago on chronic triple immunosuppression (tacrolimus, azathioprine, and prednisone), and bilateral refractive surgery for high myopia 20 years ago. Reported a history of prior unprotected sexual intercourse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for bilateral progressive visual loss, nyctalopia, central scotomas, and a faint palmar/thoracic rash; negative for ocular pain or epiphora. Home medications: tacrolimus, azathioprine, and prednisone.

objective.physical_examination: Best-corrected visual acuity dropped from 20/50 OD and 20/80 OS to 20/400 OD and 20/200 OS. Slit-lamp examination showed old refractive surgery corneal scars and mild diffuse corneal opacities OU; fundoscopy showed only myopic retinal pigment epithelium rarefaction without visible vitritis, retinitis, or vasculitis. General physical examination on hospital admission revealed a subtle erythematous maculopapular rash on both palms extending to the thorax, with no genital lesions, lymphadenopathy, or focal neurological or cardiovascular deficits.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline serum creatinine was 1.5 mg/dL, and serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Full-field electroretinography (ERG) demonstrated severe inner retinal ischemia/dysfunction. Non-contrast head CT was normal. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis of 66.3 cells/uL (100% lymphocytes), normal CSF protein and glucose, and negative cryptococcal antigen.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis and neurosyphilis presenting with occult syphilitic outer/inner retinopathy (ERG-proven retinal ischemia without overt fundoscopic chorioretinitis) in an immunosuppressed renal transplant recipient, established via extremely high serum VDRL titers (1:2,048 outpatient; 1:512 on admission), positive serum FTA-ABS, and reactive CSF VDRL with CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis (66.3 cells/uL). Treated with intravenous aqueous penicillin G 24 million IU/day for 14 days, resulting in partial ERG recovery at 4 months and recovery of visual acuity to 20/40 OD and 20/30 OS with a serum VDRL titer of 1:256 at 6-month follow-up.
